curcumin.summary: Turmeric's yellow polyphenol, taken to calm inflammation, joint soreness, puffiness and skin redness so you recover faster and look less inflamed.

quick.overview:
Curcumin is the main yellow pigment of turmeric. People take it to bring down everyday inflammation, which they link to less joint soreness after training, less facial puffiness and calmer, less red skin.

It works by dialing down inflammatory signaling (NF-κB, COX-2) and acting as an antioxidant in lab studies. Systematic reviews of trials report improvements in arthritis pain and in inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein. Skin and appearance uses have been studied far less than joint pain. Plain curcumin is poorly absorbed, so products use piperine, lipid or other delivery forms.
quick.how: Most people take it as a capsule or powder with a meal, usually in a formulation built for absorption (with black pepper extract, lipid-based or micellar forms). It is often stacked with boswellia, fish oil or other recovery supplements, and users typically run it daily for several weeks before judging joint comfort or skin changes. Turmeric is also used in cooking.
quick.risks: Generally well tolerated, with occasional stomach upset. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported with high-bioavailability products, and it can interact with anticoagulants. Supplement quality varies, and adulteration with lead-containing pigments has been documented. Legal as a dietary supplement.

angle.text: Curcumin is taken to lower inflammation, which users connect to less joint soreness, faster recovery, and less facial puffiness and skin redness. Trials have measured joint pain and inflammation markers; skin and appearance uses come mostly from user reports.

n-acetylcysteine.summary: Glutathione-building antioxidant that people take for clearer, healthier skin and to support the liver and recovery during heavy training or hormone use.

quick.overview:
N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a form of the amino acid cysteine. In appearance circles it is taken to support clearer skin and fewer breakouts, and by people on hormones or anabolic steroids as a liver-support and recovery supplement.

NAC supplies cysteine, the limiting building block for glutathione, the body's main internal antioxidant, which is how it is meant to reduce oxidative stress and inflammation in skin. It is an established medicine for acetaminophen overdose and as a mucus-thinning agent. Small studies have looked at acne, and it has been studied for compulsive-behavior conditions; evidence for skin, hair or recovery uses is limited.
quick.how: Taken as a capsule or powder, usually daily, often alongside other antioxidants or a liver-support stack. Users commonly report waiting several weeks to judge skin changes. It is sold over the counter in most places.
quick.risks: Common side effects are nausea and other digestive upset, and a sulfur smell is often noted. Intravenous use carries a risk of anaphylactoid reactions. Its US status as a supplement has been disputed because it is also an approved drug, though it remains widely available.

angle.text: NAC is taken to raise glutathione, which users link to less oxidative stress and inflammation, fewer breakouts and healthier skin; steroid users also take it for liver support. It is an established medicine for other conditions, and small studies have touched acne.

glycine.summary: The main amino acid in collagen, taken for skin, hair and nail support and for deeper sleep.

quick.overview:
Glycine makes up about a third of the amino acids in collagen, so people take it hoping to support skin, hair, nails and joints. It is also taken before bed for better sleep, which feeds into how rested and clear-skinned you look.

Glycine is a substrate for collagen, creatine and glutathione, and it acts as an inhibitory neurotransmitter that lowers core body temperature, the proposed route to better sleep. Small trials found improved subjective sleep quality. Trials of collagen hydrolysates are rich in glycine but are not tests of glycine alone, and direct evidence that it visibly changes skin is limited.
quick.how: A sweet-tasting powder, usually stirred into water or a drink in the evening, sometimes alongside magnesium or collagen. It is also eaten through gelatin, bone broth and protein foods. Users usually report on sleep within days to weeks and on skin over longer periods.
quick.risks: Very well tolerated at typical intakes; mild stomach upset or drowsiness can occur. It is a food-grade supplement with no particular legal restrictions. Interactions with some antipsychotics such as clozapine have been noted.

angle.text: Glycine is the main building block of collagen, and users take it for better skin, hair and nails and for deeper sleep, which shows up as a more rested look. Sleep studies exist; the skin benefits are reasoned from its role in collagen.

taurine.summary: Amino acid taken by lifters for training endurance, less cramping and recovery, supporting more output and muscle over time.

quick.overview:
Taurine is found in high concentrations in muscle, heart and brain. Lifters take it for endurance, fewer cramps and a calmer wind-down after hard sessions, and some steroid users take it as part of a protective stack.

The idea is that better training output and recovery add up to more muscle. Taurine contributes to cell hydration, calcium handling and antioxidant defense. Reviews report small effects on some exercise and metabolic outcomes; no study found tests it for physique or facial appearance in healthy people.
quick.how: Sold as a standalone powder or capsule and a common ingredient in energy drinks. People usually take it daily or around training and combine it with creatine, electrolytes or sleep supplements. It is also obtained from meat and fish.
quick.risks: Considered safe at typical intakes, with rare mild digestive effects. Most health concerns about energy drinks relate to caffeine rather than taurine. It is legal and sold as a supplement and food additive.

angle.text: Taurine is used for better workouts, fewer cramps and recovery, which users connect to more training output and more muscle. Exercise studies show small effects; none has tested it for appearance directly.

boswellia-serrata.summary: Indian frankincense extract taken for joint comfort and recovery so you can train harder and more often for a more muscular look.

quick.overview:
Boswellia is a resin extract taken to ease joint pain and speed recovery, so people can train more often and with less aching toward a more muscular physique.

Its boswellic acids, especially AKBA, inhibit 5-lipoxygenase and reduce leukotriene production, which lowers inflammatory signaling. Meta-analyses of knee osteoarthritis trials report improvements in pain, stiffness and function. Those trials looked at osteoarthritis, not training outcomes, and many were small and industry-linked.
quick.how: Taken as a standardized extract capsule, commonly daily and often combined with curcumin, glucosamine or fish oil. Users typically report joint changes after a few weeks. It has a long history in Ayurvedic medicine.
quick.risks: Side effects are generally mild, such as stomach upset or diarrhea. Product standardization varies, and safety in pregnancy has not been established. Legal as a dietary supplement; over-harvesting of wild trees is an ecological concern.

angle.text: Boswellia is taken to ease joint pain and speed recovery, so users can train harder and more often in pursuit of more muscle and a leaner look. Trials have studied osteoarthritis pain rather than training outcomes.

bromelain.summary: Pineapple enzyme taken to reduce swelling, bruising and puffiness, especially for faster healing after cosmetic procedures.

quick.overview:
Bromelain is a mix of protein-digesting enzymes from pineapple stem. People take it to cut down swelling and bruising after cosmetic surgery or injury, and some use it for general puffiness and inflammation.

Its enzyme activity is thought to modulate inflammatory mediators such as bradykinin and prostaglandins and affect fibrin breakdown. Systematic reviews cover post-surgical swelling and pain, osteoarthritis and other inflammatory conditions, with small, mixed trials. A topical form is approved in Europe for removing dead tissue from burns.
quick.how: Taken as capsules or tablets, often started before and continued after a procedure, or used with other recovery supplements such as arnica. Some also use it as a digestive enzyme. Potency varies between products.
quick.risks: Side effects include stomach upset and allergic reactions, especially in people allergic to pineapple. It may increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants and can interact with some antibiotics. Supplement potency is inconsistent. Legal as a supplement.

angle.text: Bromelain is taken to reduce swelling and bruising, notably after surgery or injury, so puffiness fades and healing looks faster. Studies have examined post-surgical swelling with mixed results; everyday facial puffiness use is anecdotal.

nmn.summary: NAD+ precursor taken, or applied in skincare, for more cellular energy and younger-looking skin.

quick.overview:
NMN is a molecule the body converts into NAD+, a coenzyme central to energy metabolism. People take it, and sometimes apply it topically, to support cellular energy and a younger-looking complexion.

NAD+ levels fall with age in several tissues, which is the rationale for supplying precursors. NMN feeds the NAD salvage pathway, and NAD+ fuels sirtuins and DNA-repair enzymes. Human trials show oral NMN raises blood NAD levels and is tolerated over weeks to months, with more modest results for functional outcomes; visible skin effects in people have not been shown.
quick.how: Usually taken as a capsule or powder, daily, often with other longevity supplements such as resveratrol or quercetin. Some skincare products include it. Users commonly report energy changes over weeks.
quick.risks: Short-term trials report good tolerability, with mild digestive upset or flushing possible. Long-term safety has not been established, and theoretical concerns about raising NAD+ in existing cancers remain open. Product quality varies. Its US supplement status has been contested.

angle.text: NMN raises the supply of NAD+, which supports cellular energy and repair, and users hope that shows up as younger-looking skin and more energy. NAD+ biochemistry is well established; human trials have measured NAD levels rather than visible aging.

nicotinamide-riboside.summary: Vitamin B3-based NAD+ booster taken for cellular energy and a younger, healthier-looking appearance.

quick.overview:
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a form of vitamin B3 that raises NAD+. People take it to support energy and slower aging, which they connect to healthier, younger-looking skin.

NR is converted to NMN and then to NAD+, supporting sirtuin and DNA-repair activity. Randomized trials consistently show it raises blood NAD+ metabolites, and trials in several conditions have mostly established tolerability. A 2023 review found it unclear whether raising NAD+ improves function in people, and appearance effects have not been tested.
quick.how: Taken as a daily capsule, often in longevity stacks alongside resveratrol, quercetin or NMN. Users usually report energy effects over several weeks.
quick.risks: Well tolerated in studies, with mild nausea, flushing or digestive effects at higher intakes. Long-term safety data are limited. It has GRAS status in the US and novel food approval in the EU; product quality varies.

angle.text: Nicotinamide riboside is taken to raise NAD+, which users link to cellular energy, slower aging and a younger look. Human studies show it raises NAD+; visible aging effects have not been tested.

resveratrol.summary: Grape-skin polyphenol taken for anti-aging skin support and, by some, as a claimed estrogen-lowering aromatase inhibitor for a leaner look.

quick.overview:
Resveratrol is a polyphenol found in grape skins, berries and peanuts. People take it to slow visible aging and keep skin looking younger, and some in bodybuilding circles use it as a claimed natural aromatase inhibitor to keep estrogen down for a leaner look. It also appears in some skincare.

It became known through lab work showing it activates sirtuins and extends lifespan in some organisms. Proposed mechanisms include SIRT1 and AMPK activation plus antioxidant effects. Human trials show small effects on some metabolic markers, and oral bioavailability of the free compound is below 1 percent because of heavy metabolism.
quick.how: Taken as a daily capsule, often with fat for absorption, and commonly stacked with NMN, NR or quercetin. Forum users discuss it alongside testosterone therapy. Topical products are also sold.
quick.risks: Usually well tolerated; high intakes can cause digestive upset. It may interact with anticoagulants and drugs metabolized by CYP enzymes. Legal as a supplement; product quality varies.

angle.text: Resveratrol is taken for anti-aging and for a claimed aromatase-inhibiting effect that would keep estrogen low, and it appears in some skincare. Lifespan findings come largely from lab organisms; human trials have looked at metabolic markers.

spermidine.summary: Autophagy-linked polyamine from wheat germ and foods, taken for slower aging and, by some, healthier hair and skin.

quick.overview:
Spermidine is a natural polyamine found in wheat germ, soybeans, mushrooms and aged cheese. People take it to support cellular cleanup (autophagy) and slower aging, and some report better hair and aging skin.

It induces autophagy in model organisms, and a 2009 paper reported lifespan extension in yeast, flies, worms and human immune cells. Laboratory work found it promoted hair shaft elongation in cultured hair follicles. Observational data link higher dietary intake to lower mortality; randomized human trials are few and small, and none has tested cosmetic outcomes.
quick.how: Usually taken as a wheat germ extract capsule or powder, daily, or through diet. Users treat it as a long-term longevity supplement and report on it over months.
quick.risks: Generally well tolerated at studied intakes; mild digestive effects are possible. Polyamines are also needed by rapidly growing cells, so theoretical concerns exist in cancer settings. Legal as a supplement or novel food in many regions.

angle.text: Spermidine is taken to trigger autophagy, the cell renewal process, which users link to slower visible aging and, in some claims, hair growth. Human studies are preliminary and have focused on cognition and health markers.

urolithin-a.summary: Gut-derived compound taken to renew mitochondria and improve muscle endurance and cellular health with age.

quick.overview:
Urolithin A is formed by gut bacteria from compounds in pomegranate, walnuts and berries. People take it as a supplement for muscle function and mitochondrial health, linking that to a stronger, younger-feeling body and training capacity.

It was identified as a compound that induces mitophagy, the clearance of damaged mitochondria. Randomized trials in older and middle-aged adults report improvements in some muscle endurance measures, with modest or mixed effects on whole-body outcomes; most trials were sponsored by the commercial supplier. Only some people produce it efficiently, which is the rationale for direct supplements. No trial has tested appearance.
quick.how: Taken as a daily capsule or powder, often as a branded form, and discussed alongside training and other longevity supplements. Trials ran for months.
quick.risks: Short-term trials report good tolerability. Long-term safety data are limited. It has GRAS status in the US and regulatory status elsewhere varies.

angle.text: Urolithin A is taken to support mitochondrial renewal, which users link to better muscle endurance, training capacity and a younger body. Early trials in older adults measured muscle endurance; appearance outcomes have not been tested.

coenzyme-q10.summary: Cellular energy cofactor and antioxidant taken or applied to skin for a younger-looking, less wrinkled complexion.

quick.overview:
CoQ10 is a molecule your body makes that carries electrons in mitochondrial energy production and acts as an antioxidant. People take it orally and apply it in creams for younger-looking skin and more energy, and some on statins take it because statins are proposed to lower its levels.

Levels fall with age. Topically it has been studied for reducing oxidative damage in skin, mostly in small studies. Its best-studied uses are cardiovascular, such as the Q-SYMBIO heart failure trial, plus statin muscle symptoms and migraine.
quick.how: Taken as a softgel with a fat-containing meal, as ubiquinone or ubiquinol, or applied as an ingredient in anti-aging creams. Users typically run it daily for weeks to months.
quick.risks: Generally well tolerated, with occasional digestive upset or insomnia. It may reduce the effect of warfarin. Legal as a supplement; the FDA does not approve it for any condition, and absorption and quality vary by formulation.

angle.text: CoQ10 supports mitochondrial energy and protects cells as an antioxidant, and users take or apply it for healthier, less wrinkled skin. Heart and statin-related uses are better studied than cosmetic ones.

alpha-lipoic-acid.summary: Antioxidant taken by lifters and dieters for better carb handling and a leaner look, and for skin health.

quick.overview:
Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) is a cofactor for mitochondrial enzymes and a redox-active antioxidant. Lifters and dieters take it for insulin sensitivity and carb partitioning, hoping for a leaner, fuller physique, and others use it for skin health and in skincare.

ALA and its reduced form scavenge reactive oxygen species, regenerate other antioxidants, and may influence insulin signaling. It has been used as a non-prescription drug for diabetic neuropathy in Germany since 1966, though a 2024 Cochrane review of long placebo-controlled trials described little or no effect on symptoms. No large trials of oral ALA for cosmetic outcomes were identified.
quick.how: Taken as a capsule, often with carbohydrate-containing meals by people using it for carb handling, and sometimes as the R-enantiomer form. Also found in some skincare serums.
quick.risks: Generally well tolerated; nausea, rash and, rarely, low blood sugar in people on glucose-lowering drugs can occur. Legal as a supplement.

angle.text: ALA is used for better glucose handling and nutrient partitioning, which users connect to a leaner, fuller-looking physique, and as an antioxidant for skin. Glucose and nerve studies exist; appearance effects have been studied little.

fisetin.summary: Strawberry flavonoid taken as a senolytic candidate for slower aging and younger-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Fisetin is a flavonol in strawberries, apples and onions. People take it as a senolytic, a compound proposed to clear aged senescent cells, hoping for healthier aging and younger-looking skin; some also claim fat loss and UV skin protection.

A 2018 paper reported fisetin extended health and lifespan in mice and reduced senescent-cell burden and inflammatory signaling. Human data are limited to small or early-phase trials, several registered but not yet reporting, and no published human trial has tested skin, hair or facial appearance. Oral bioavailability is described as low.
quick.how: Taken as a capsule, usually in short periodic bursts rather than continuously, as the senolytic approach describes, and often stacked with quercetin. Product formulations aimed at absorption are sold.
quick.risks: Human safety data at the amounts discussed online are sparse, and drug interactions are not well characterized. Legal as a supplement, but not an approved therapy for any condition.

angle.text: Fisetin is taken as a senolytic, meant to clear aged cells, which users link to slower aging and younger-looking skin. The evidence comes mostly from animal and cell studies.

quercetin.summary: Antioxidant flavonoid taken for calmer, less inflamed skin and as a senolytic partner for anti-aging.

quick.overview:
Quercetin is a flavonol found in onions, capers and apples. People take it as an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory for calmer skin and less puffiness, and it is the 'Q' in the dasatinib plus quercetin senolytic combination studied in aging research.

It shows antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity and mast-cell stabilizing in lab studies. Small early-phase trials of the dasatinib plus quercetin combination ran in conditions such as pulmonary fibrosis and diabetic kidney disease, but they use a cancer drug alongside it and cannot show what quercetin does alone. Oral absorption is low, and no clinical study of skin, hair or facial appearance was identified.
quick.how: Taken as a capsule, often with other polyphenols or in longevity stacks, and commonly paired with fisetin in senolytic-style routines. Some choose bioavailability-enhanced forms.
quick.risks: Usually well tolerated at supplement amounts; high intakes may cause headache or stomach upset and could affect kidney function or drug metabolism. Legal as a supplement.

angle.text: Quercetin is taken as an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory for calmer skin and less puffiness, and, with dasatinib in research, as a senolytic. Senolytic trials are early; appearance-specific effects have not been studied.

rapamycin.summary: Prescription mTOR inhibitor used off-label by longevity enthusiasts to slow aging, with topical versions explored for skin rejuvenation.

quick.overview:
Rapamycin (sirolimus) is a prescription immunosuppressant that some longevity enthusiasts use off-label to slow aging and keep a younger look, and it is explored topically for skin rejuvenation.

It inhibits mTORC1, a nutrient-sensing growth pathway, which promotes autophagy and reduces growth signaling. It is among the best-replicated lifespan-extending drugs in mice. A 2024 systematic review of 19 human studies found improvements in some physiological aging parameters in immune, cardiovascular and skin systems, with increased infections and raised cholesterol and triglycerides in people with age-related diseases. It is approved for transplant rejection, certain rare diseases and, topically, facial angiofibromas.
quick.how: Used only with a prescription, under physician supervision, off-label, and typically on an intermittent schedule in longevity communities, often with regular blood work. Topical forms are used in skin experiments.
quick.risks: Prescription-only. Known adverse effects include mouth ulcers, impaired wound healing, raised lipids, glucose intolerance and increased infection risk, particularly at transplant levels. Off-label use for longevity is not approved.

angle.text: Rapamycin inhibits mTOR, a growth pathway linked to aging, and users hope it keeps skin and body looking younger. Lifespan extension is shown in animals; it is an immunosuppressant with known side effects.

metformin.summary: Diabetes drug used off-label for belly fat, carb handling, acne and anti-aging, and to manage blood sugar during hormone use.

quick.overview:
Metformin is a first-line type 2 diabetes drug. Some people use it off-label to cut belly fat, handle carbs better, calm acne and slow aging, and to manage blood sugar during testosterone or growth hormone use.

It lowers liver glucose output and improves insulin sensitivity, partly through AMPK activation, which is the chain toward less fat storage and possibly clearer skin. It has decades of safety data in diabetes, and observational studies in diabetics link it to lower cancer risk and mortality. Reviews in 2021 and 2025 take a cautious view of its effect on aging in people without diabetes, and some evidence suggests it may blunt exercise adaptations.
quick.how: Taken as a daily tablet with meals under a prescription, often ramped up gradually to limit digestive effects. Forum users discuss it for body composition and alongside hormone therapy, sometimes sourcing it from overseas pharmacies.
quick.risks: Common side effects are digestive upset, and vitamin B12 deficiency can develop with long-term use; rare lactic acidosis occurs mainly with kidney impairment. It may blunt muscle growth and endurance gains. Prescription-only in the US, UK and EU; off-label use for aging is not approved.

angle.text: Metformin lowers glucose and insulin, which users link to better carb handling, less belly fat and possibly clearer skin. It is established for diabetes; appearance uses have been studied lightly, and some report it may blunt muscle growth.

epitalon.summary: Synthetic peptide promoted for telomere lengthening and slower aging, which users connect to a younger look.

quick.overview:
Epitalon is a synthetic four-amino-acid peptide, developed from a bovine pineal gland extract, that is promoted for lengthening telomeres and slowing aging, which users connect to younger-looking skin and body.

Lab work from the originating St. Petersburg group reports it raises telomere length in human cell lines through telomerase upregulation or an alternative lengthening mechanism, and it has been proposed to affect melatonin production. Russian clinical reports claim effects on aging markers. Large independent placebo-controlled human trials have not been published.
quick.how: Sold as a research chemical and discussed in peptide stack forums, usually in periodic courses rather than continuous use. Product quality and identity are not independently verified.
quick.risks: Human safety data are small and mostly from one research group. It is not approved as a drug by major regulators, products are unregulated, and telomerase activation raises theoretical cancer concerns.

angle.text: Epitalon is promoted as a telomere-lengthening peptide that slows cellular aging, which users connect to a younger appearance. Research comes mainly from one Russian group, with cell-line and animal work.

mots-c.summary: Mitochondria-derived peptide used as an exercise mimetic, aimed at fat loss and leaner body composition.

quick.overview:
MOTS-c is a short peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA that rises with exercise. Users run it in peptide stacks as an exercise mimetic to burn fat, build endurance and reverse age-related decline, sometimes alongside GLP-1 drugs.

In mice it promoted metabolic balance and reduced obesity and insulin resistance, acting on the folate-methionine cycle and AMPK, and it moves to the nucleus under stress to influence gene expression. Human data are limited to observational studies of circulating levels, early-phase studies of a synthetic analogue and a registered phase 2 trial in prediabetes.
quick.how: Sold as a research chemical, discussed in peptide-stacking communities in cycled courses combined with training and diet. Product identity and purity are not independently verified.
quick.risks: Human safety data for vendor products are essentially absent. It is not an approved drug and has been named as prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency since 2024; gray-market purity is unreliable.

angle.text: MOTS-c is used as an exercise mimetic that users hope improves glucose and fat metabolism for a leaner body, sometimes alongside GLP-1 drugs. Findings so far are from mice, with little human data on appearance.

ss-31.summary: Mitochondria-targeted peptide used for cellular energy, skin anti-aging and wound healing; approved only for Barth syndrome.

quick.overview:
SS-31 (elamipretide) is a mitochondria-targeted peptide. Peptide enthusiasts use it for cellular energy, cosmetic skin anti-aging and faster wound healing.

It binds cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is thought to stabilize respiratory complexes, improve electron transport and reduce reactive oxygen species. The FDA granted accelerated approval in September 2025 for improving muscle strength in Barth syndrome, a rare mitochondrial disease. It was also studied in mitochondrial myopathy, heart failure and macular degeneration with mixed results; no published trial has tested it in healthy people for appearance.
quick.how: The approved drug is given under medical supervision to patients. Outside that, gray-market research-chemical versions circulate in peptide communities for energy and longevity, with no standard protocol.
quick.risks: Reported adverse events in trials are mostly injection-site reactions. Long-term safety has not been fully established, and vendor products are unregulated and may differ from the approved drug. Approval covers one rare disease, not general use.

angle.text: SS-31 targets mitochondria to improve cellular energy, which peptide users link to younger-looking skin and faster wound healing. It is approved only for Barth syndrome; cosmetic use in healthy people has not been tested.
